headline: Europe agrees a GS1 unit-dose barcode roadmap for hospital medicines; the UK still has no plan
executive_summary: This Monday-to-Monday week is quieter than Friday’s first live digest, and that is the finding rather than a gap. The only new development that passed the GS1 UK relevance test is a European hospital-and-industry agreement, published on 7 September, that every in-scope hospital medicine should carry a GS1 DataMatrix at unit-dose level – GTIN only as a minimum, GTIN plus batch and expiry as the preferred form – with new launches from 2031 and coverage targets out to 2041. The Royal College of Pharmacy told The Pharmaceutical Journal on 9 September that there are no plans to introduce single-unit coding in the UK, even though EAHP’s membership includes Great Britain and NHS pharmacists say the absence of a scannable code at the bedside is already blocking barcode medicines administration. GS1 UK’s healthcare lead used the announcement to restress Scan4Safety, GTIN/DataMatrix quality and the House of Lords medicines-security findings on missing UK pack codes. Nothing new was laid this week on DRS barcodes, construction-product identifiers, GB UDI, packaging EPR labelling, Windsor Framework marks or Sunrise 2027. Last week’s operational clocks still run: DRS one-year countdown from 1 October 2026, CBAM verification from 1 January 2027, and MHCLG’s construction-product data-library discovery this quarter. The UK digital product records call for evidence closes at 23:59 on 21 September – seven days from this digest – and remains the last structured chance this month to argue for a single data carrier interoperable with the EU DPP.
cross_sector_themes: A European industry standard can lock GTIN and GS1 DataMatrix in without a UK legal mandate – and the UK can still be left without an equivalent plan
2027 remains the UK operational year (DRS, CBAM, construction GSR, GB UDI) while this week’s new hospital-medicines timeline starts only in 2031
Unit-of-use identification is moving from outer pack to the dose, blister, vial or syringe – the same layer Scan4Safety and closed-loop medicines management already need
The UK digital product records call for evidence still closes on 21 September 2026; no government update landed this week

sector_overviews.headline: No new retail identification or labelling instrument this week; DRS and the DPR deadline remain the live work
sector_overviews.summary: Retail had no new statutory instrument, scheme announcement or guidance that passed the GS1 UK relevance test between 7 and 14 September, once last week’s DRS countdown briefing and CBAM emissions-and-verification regulations are left in the 11 September archive. Exchange for Change did not publish the product-testing guidelines it had promised by September, nor the first certified reverse-vending-machine list (still indicated for early October). PackUK’s 1 September cut-off for 2025 packaging-data resubmissions that affect 2026/27 notices of liability has now passed, with fees still due later this year. OPSS added only a routine General Product Safety designated-standards proposal on 9 September. Members should treat this as a planning week, not an empty one: the UK digital product records call for evidence still closes on 21 September, and drinks SKUs still need GTIN, artwork and Article List work before the 1 October 2026 one-year DRS mark.

sector_overviews.headline: No new construction-product identifier, golden-thread or GSR text this week
sector_overviews.summary: Construction is silent this week. MHCLG, the Building Safety Regulator and OPSS published no new consultation response, statutory instrument or digital-library specification after the 10 September Grenfell progress report already covered in the 11 September digest. That report still stands: government responses to the Construction Products Reform White Paper and General Safety Requirement consultations later in 2026, GSR legislation when parliamentary time allows, and a digital discovery for a construction-product information library in this quarter. PAS 2000:2026 and CCPI were not updated. Construction members who also export to the EU still sit on the ESPR/DPP and (from 18 February 2027) battery-passport clocks; those files did not move this week either. The practical task remains to put GTIN, GS1 Digital Link and product-record language into MHCLG’s live discovery and into the UK DPR call for evidence before 21 September.

sector_overviews.headline: Europe sets a GTIN/DataMatrix unit-dose plan from 2031; the UK says it is not following
sector_overviews.summary: Healthcare is the only sector with a new keep this week. On 7 September EAHP and EFPIA published joint implementation guidance that hospital medicines should carry a GS1 DataMatrix at each vial, blister pocket, syringe or other single unit, using GTIN as the sole product identifier and, where pack space allows, batch/lot (AI 10) and expiry (AI 17). New hospital-relevant launches would use the advanced form from 2031; 50% of in-scope products by 2036 and 80% by 2041; hospitals themselves are targeted for 50% bedside-scan capability by 2032. This is industry guidance, not UK law. The Royal College of Pharmacy confirmed on 9 September that single-unit coding is not planned for the UK, even as NHS chief pharmacists told The Pharmaceutical Journal that missing bedside codes are already forcing unsafe workarounds. GS1 UK tied the text to Scan4Safety, closed-loop medicines management and last month’s trust survey on missing pack DataMatrix. No new GB UDI, MDOR, Scan4Safety IMS or implant-card instrument landed. The draft Medical Devices (Amendment) Regulations 2026 remain the December 2026 file to watch.

items.title: EAHP and EFPIA publish GS1 DataMatrix unit-dose roadmap from 2031 – no UK plan yet
items.issuing_body: European Association of Hospital Pharmacists (EAHP) / European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA)
items.summary: On 7 September 2026 EAHP and EFPIA published joint guidance requiring a GS1 DataMatrix on each hospital unit dose, with GTIN as the only product identifier. New in-scope launches would carry GTIN, batch and expiry from 2031. The Royal College of Pharmacy has confirmed there is no UK implementation plan.
items.what_changed:
EAHP and EFPIA published 'Single Unit Coding – Joint EFPIA and EAHP Guidance for Implementation' on 7 September 2026 (EFPIA Board approval 25 March 2026; EAHP Board endorsement January 2026). The document extends FMD-style pack coding down to the single unit of use – vials, bottles, blisters, pre-filled syringes, pens, sachets, ampoules and cartridges – for products with strong relevance to the hospital market.

Design rules are explicit and GS1-only. The product identifier is exclusively the GTIN; the guidance says there is 'strictly no deviation from the GS1 standards' of the kind once permitted in the European Medicines Verification System, and 'no scope for national derivatives'. The data carrier is a GS1 DataMatrix. Three forms are defined: Basic (GTIN only, AI 01), used where pack space or process cannot support more; Advanced (GTIN, batch/lot AI 10 and expiry AI 17 in YYMMDD); and Advanced+ (Advanced plus human-readable elements where national rules require them). A serial number is not required at unit-dose level. GTIN assignment must follow the GS1 Healthcare GTIN Allocation Rules; each single unit of use gets a GTIN unique to that presentation, which can be shared across different sales-pack sizes.

Timing is counted from 25 March 2026: all new in-scope product launches from 2031 must use Advanced coding; 50% of in-scope products by 2036 and 80% by 2041 must use Basic or Advanced; a progress-monitoring method should exist by March 2028. Hospital-side targets are 50% of European hospitals able to bedside-scan Basic codes by 2032, then 80% Basic and 50% Advanced by 2036. EAHP represents hospital pharmacists in 37 countries including Great Britain. The Royal College of Pharmacy told The Pharmaceutical Journal on 9 September that single-unit coding 'is not currently planned for implementation in the UK'. FMD 2D barcodes have not been mandatory in Great Britain since 31 December 2020, nor in Northern Ireland since 1 January 2025.
items.why_it_matters_to_gs1:
This is the clearest industry-written specification GS1 UK has seen this year for medicines identification below pack level, and it names GS1 keys and the GS1 DataMatrix as the only acceptable design. It is not UK law and must not be reported as a new MHRA duty. It still matters because UK marketing-authorisation holders who supply hospitals in EAHP countries will be asked for a unit-dose GTIN and DataMatrix on those SKUs from 2031, while NHS trusts already cannot run barcode medicines administration or closed-loop dispensing when the code stops at the outer pack. Iain Davidson, chief pharmacist at Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust, told The Pharmaceutical Journal that missing bedside codes produce poor scan rates or unsafe workarounds, and that original-pack dispensing in the NHS makes manufacturer-applied unit-dose codes 'a crucial step forward'. GS1 UK’s Georgina Lawton tied the text to Scan4Safety, NHS digital medicines programmes and the House of Lords medicines-security report on missing, inaccurate or unreadable UK pack barcodes – the same gap GS1 UK’s August trust survey quantified (57% of trusts reporting moderate-to-severe pharmacy disruption).

If GS1 UK does nothing, European hospitals will standardise on GTIN/DataMatrix at dose level while GB packs remain a mixed, often linear-only, estate, and Scan4Safety / GSRN wristband scanning will still have nothing reliable to match at administration. If members do nothing, UK hospital SKUs sold into the EU will need a second artwork and GTIN-allocation programme at short notice, and NHS trusts will keep re-labelling or skipping scans. The opportunity is to use this text, with the August survey, to press DHSC, MHRA and the four chief pharmaceutical officers for a GB policy that at least preserves FMD-equivalent pack DataMatrix and sets a hospital unit-dose direction aligned with GS1 Healthcare rules.
